subsection: 3. Using the table as a predictive guide

notes.b: Each element's box and position give information about its atoms and its behaviour.
points: Each box gives the symbol, atomic number and relative atomic mass of an element.
The atomic number gives the number of protons and, in a neutral atom, the number of electrons.
The group gives the element's outer-electron arrangement (see "Groups, periods and blocks").
The period gives the number of occupied energy levels.
The element's position relative to the staircase line shows whether it is a metal, non-metal or metalloid.

notes.b: Elements in the same group share an outer-electron arrangement, so they behave in similar ways.
points: Reactions can be predicted from a group: sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, so potassium, in the same group, will react with water in the same way, giving potassium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Group 1 elements form 1⁺ ions, group 2 elements form 2⁺ ions and group 13 elements form 3⁺ ions.
Group 15 elements form 3⁻ ions, group 16 elements form 2⁻ ions and group 17 elements form 1⁻ ions.
Noble gases (group 18) have full outer energy levels and are very unreactive.

notes.b: The formula of a compound follows from the charges of its ions, which must balance to give no overall charge.
points: Magnesium (group 2) forms Mg²⁺ and chlorine (group 17) forms Cl⁻, so two chloride ions balance one magnesium ion and the formula is MgCl₂.
Aluminium (group 13) forms Al³⁺ and oxygen (group 16) forms O²⁻, so two aluminium ions balance three oxide ions and the formula is Al₂O₃.

notes.b: Trends in the table allow properties of unfamiliar elements to be estimated from their neighbours.
points: Properties change gradually and predictably down a group and across a period, so an unknown property can be estimated from neighbouring elements.
Astatine (At, atomic number 85) lies at the bottom of group 17; from the trend in the halogens it is predicted to be a dark solid that is less reactive than iodine.
Mendeleev used the same approach to predict the properties of undiscovered elements (see "Development of the modern periodic table").
Every trend is explained by electron arrangement: the number of outer electrons, the number of occupied energy levels and the nuclear charge.

keyTerms.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element, shown in the box for that element.
The mass of an element's atoms relative to other atoms, shown in the box for that element.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.
The charge on an ion of an element, predicted from its group, which determines the formulae of its compounds.
A gradual and predictable change in a property down a group or across a period of the periodic table.
The arrangement of noble gases, which makes them very unreactive.

questions.prompt: Use the periodic table to predict the formula of the compound formed between (i) calcium and fluorine, (ii) aluminium and sulfur, and explain how you made each prediction.
questions.model: (i) Calcium is in group 2, so it forms Ca²⁺ ions. Fluorine is in group 17, so it forms F⁻ ions. One calcium ion balances two fluoride ions, so the formula is CaF₂. (ii) Aluminium is in group 13, so it forms Al³⁺ ions. Sulfur is in group 16, so it forms S²⁻ ions. Two aluminium ions balance three sulfide ions, so the formula is Al₂S₃.

questions.prompt: Rubidium is in group 1 below potassium. Predict two properties of rubidium and explain your predictions.
questions.model: Rubidium is more reactive than potassium, reacting more vigorously with water to give rubidium hydroxide (RbOH) and hydrogen. Both elements are in group 1 and have one outer electron, so they react in similar ways; reactivity increases down the group because rubidium has more occupied energy levels, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily. Rubidium forms Rb⁺ ions, because it has one outer electron, which it loses to form an ion with a 1⁺ charge.
